in writing. ‒ i congratulate ms berès on the report on economic governance. it has been a very complex process and the rapporteur managed to give an excellent overview and made valuable comments. i especially agree with the observation that economic governance has become so complex that it has started to work against us. it has indeed a detrimental effect on transparency and democracy. i welcome the fact that the report calls for less complexity, more transparency and identifies a european-wide measure against tax fraud and evasion and aggressive corporate tax planning as a tool to achieve it. the country-by-country reporting for corporates was also mentioned in the report, which was unfortunately not introduced by the commission’s action plan for a fairer corporate tax system. i urge the stakeholders to take note of the recommendations of the report and aim for a less complicated economic governance system that could stabilise the current fragile economic situation.
member of the commission.– mr president, the resolution and the debate we have had this afternoon sum up very well the main points that we are trying to achieve. i just want to highlight four or five of the main themes that have come up this afternoon. first of all, in terms of building from the bottom up, identifying barriers and obstacles and knocking them down, and building the capital markets union with people, rather than doing things to people: that is how i am approaching it. and that is why support for the capital markets union is very strong, as it happens, in the city of london – because they see the benefits that come to britain from being part of a large single market. i think it is wrong to misrepresent the views of people in the city of london. in terms of some of the other issues that were raised, i think we need to identify and overcome these barriers. we need to be proportionate in our regulation and in how we regulate. the regulation that has been passed is clearly linked with the flow of capital through the union. some specific points were raised about insolvency, taxation and private pensions. these issues are addressed in the green paper. we asked questions about insolvency and taxation, and we will follow those up in our response to it. we are considering a specific recommendation to do with the idea of having a voluntary ‘29th regime’ to encourage personal pensions. so a number of the points that have been raised are indeed being addressed. it is also important to emphasise that the point of what we are trying to do is to complement the funding streams we already have and to add to the banking system. if you have a system – which we have in europe – which is heavily dependent on one source of funding – the banking system – and you have a contraction in the banking system, then you get the consequences we have seen: of businesses in the economy not getting the funding they need. i feel strongly that, if we can diversify sources of funding and give small, medium-sized and large businesses alternative sources of funding, we can make a contribution to growth and to creating new jobs. there is support for this way forward. i welcome the support i have had, and i welcome the arguments set out in the resolution. we have an opportunity to make some progress. i do not claim this is the holy grail, but i do claim that we have an opportunity now to do what we set out to do over 50 years ago, which is to achieve the free movement of capital. i hope that we can now make some further progress on the back of this proposal.
first vice-president of the commission. – mr president, i will only take a few minutes of your time to tell you a few things before vice-president katainen takes over. first of all, this commission remains strongly committed to presenting – before this parliament and before the end of the year – a circular economy package which has a holistic approach on the issue – yes, on waste, but also on the re—use of finite materials and on other proposals that would create the environment for a new economy for europe. why do we need this, and why do we passionately believe in this? because the future of the european economy is not in competing on low wages; the future of the european economy is not in competing on creating stuff with finite resources. the future of the european economy is in the circular economy – in reusing, in putting things back into the economic cycle, and in thinking in terms of cradle to cradle. funnily enough, businesses have got this more – and got it better – than we have as politicians. businesses are leading on this, and we should be leading, as well, as politicians. why? because we know where we are. we also know where we need to be, which is in the circular economy, but we do not know well how to get from where we are to where we need to be. and here is where politics needs to lead; here is where government comes in, and here is where the european union is an essential link in getting us from where we are to where we need to be. i passionately believe in this transition. i believe this year, by presenting our package, we can make the first important contribution to this transformation (which is inevitable), and the report we discussed today is an important building block for what we are going to do. indeed, we will look at the waste package, as i have said, and we will work on it so that we can present the new waste package before the end of the year – and, essentially, we will look at all the other issues we need for the circular economy. i believe in this because it is a huge business opportunity for european businesses. it is also a huge opportunity for the european economy and for jobs. that is why vice-president katainen and i work on this closely with all our colleagues – commissioner bieńkowska, commissioner vella, and many others – because we take a holistic approach. i would encourage parliament to look at this, not within silos, but as something we have a common interest in, because a circular economy is not something we do just for the environment. sustainability, of course, has an environmental angle, but sustainability has, especially, an economic and a social angle. if we do not take the three elements into account – economic, social and environmental sustainability – we will not succeed in creating the right conditions for the circular economy. i want to stress this. why are businesses interested in this? because it is the most interesting business model for the future; because they know it is sustainable; because they know it will lead to growth; because they know this is where europe can lead worldwide. we should use that opportunity to integrate the three elements of sustainability – economic, social and environmental – and then, i believe, we will be successful. you can count on the commission to take this holistic approach; you can count on the commission to work closely with you. i am sure that we can look at the elements, particularly starting with analysing the situation in member states and having comparable analyses from them, so that we can take it from the zero situation to the higher levels in the next couple of years. the commission will certainly be part of that transition.
vice-president of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, thank you very much for giving us the chance to discuss this very topical and important issue. as you heard, the commission strongly believes in the circular economy. the circular economy will be a megatrend in the world economy similar to globalisation. the current linear model is not sustainable or reasonable from an economic, environmental or societal point of view. for instance, if you look at the car sector, the average car is parked around 90% of the time. if you look at office buildings, office buildings are empty some 50% of the time. so we have to look at the economy from a different angle than we have done before. as vice-president timmermans has just said, we have to look at the circular economy from a wider perspective. it is not only about recycling or waste, but we should focus on this as a complete concept in the market economy. that is why we need to find the right incentives for the business sector to further develop their business models. we also we have to find the right incentives for consumers to change their consumer behaviour and, by doing so, lead development by their own choices. at the moment the business sector is leading the circular economy, and this is a very good thing. as a regulator, we have to find the right things to support this development. we need the input of stakeholders in order to define what needs to be regulated – or even deregulated; how we can use the tools we have at eu level to promote better use of our resources and how we can strengthen the circular economy as an integral part of the dynamic market economy. we must also be careful not to overregulate everything. this is often a problem for a regulator, who may, even in good faith, sometimes do so. the ‘report on resource efficiency: moving towards a circular economy’, as approved in the committee on the environment, public health and food safety (envi) last month, sets the bar high. we appreciate and take note of your ambitious proposals. i would like to comment on some of the many issues your report raises. let me start by what we call the other half of the circle. the commission shares your view that product design is of paramount importance in getting things right from the start. there is the potential for an increased focus on circular aspects in order to design products that are made to last and that can be remanufactured and repaired easily, thus facilitating high-quality recycling. we are looking closely into this matter. we see a strong role for public procurement in creating demand for sustainable products, and we are examining the contribution that can be made by green public procurement in this respect. on buildings, we thank parliament for its support for a more holistic approach to resource efficiency throughout the full life-cycle of buildings. to avoid burden shifting, we need to look at overall impacts beyond energy efficiency. the upcoming revised legislative proposal on waste is expected to focus on stepping up implementation on the ground and to take account of different levels of current performance in individual member states, while keeping a high and achievable level of vision on recycling. it will be essential to base this work on sound evidence. another important viewpoint is that member states and stakeholders see real added value in cooperating at eu level to tackle food waste. to that end, we will closely examine possibilities for preventing food waste. to conclude, my mandate is to look at all the work we are doing in the circular economy from the perspective of growth, jobs, competitiveness and investment. i know that, if designed right, we can enable a triple win. first, there are economic gains to be made from using raw materials and resources more efficiently and being less dependent on imports. secondly, there are environmental gains in moving away from a linear economy where we throw away products that could be repaired or recycled. thirdly, there are social gains to be made from preventing waste and further improving local waste management, recycling, repair and reuse services.
rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on industry, research and energy.– mr president, as rapporteur of the committee on industry, research and energy (itre), i would like to say thank you to sirpa pietikäinen, rapporteur for the committee on the environment, public health and food safety (envi) report, and i would like to stress that the itre opinion, which was accepted with a huge majority, is clearly in line and supports everything which is included in the envi position. i would like just to point out some important elements of our opinion. the first part is that we clearly need an ambitious new package from the commission as soon as possible, which includes quantitative targets, not just wishes and also which has legislative parts. we need clear targets and legislative proposals to step ahead in the circular economy. concerning some specific issues in the itre committee, we would like to emphasise the importance of the following: incentivising both reuse and preparations for reuse through quantitative targets; a fiscal framework in accordance with the ‘polluter pays’ principle; addressing the production side (which was mentioned already by commissioner katainen); better production design standards to make products more durable and easier to assemble, and so on; and the fight against planned obsolescence in order to protect consumers.

mr president, resource and energy efficiency is not just a green issue. the competitiveness of europe's economy and industry today depends primarily on progress in energy and resource efficiency. the increasingly wasteful use of resources, the increasingly dramatic increase in europe's energy consumption, could lead us to an economic dead end. we are already the world's number one energy importer, importing more than half of our total energy needs. this kind of energy dependency can only be reduced by the member states working together in alliance with europe. this is particularly true in the area of energy poverty, which is a growing problem, particularly in central and eastern europe. i am therefore convinced that improving energy efficiency, creating a common european energy union, can lead to low and sustainable energy bills, rather than to the imposition of official price controls by individual member states for domestic consumption, and that is why we must support the commission's proposal to develop a union energy efficiency index.

in writing. following the abolition of the milk quota in april, milk producers are even more exposed to fluctuations in world milk prices and to commercial practices in international food chains that in many cases are detrimental to producers. it is therefore essential for the european union to protect the interests of milk producers and to strengthen the milk sector. my colleague james nicholson, the northern ireland representative, has put a report on the table that is focused on production. i agree with him that the policy of the milk package based on producer organisations and strengthening the bargaining position of producers is the way forward. in addition, special efforts should be made to protect milk producers in disadvantaged areas and in mountain areas. the amounts deducted from the milk levy should be kept within the agricultural budget and used to support the competitiveness of the milk sector. the authorisations of producer organisations should be further strengthened and their influence on the drawing up of collective supply contracts should be further increased. the performance of the milk monitoring centre needs to be improved. it is a significant success for hungary that both of my proposals to increase the efficiency of crisis management were included in the report. the european commission should be invited to adjust the intervention prices to reflect the real market price and production costs. in addition, in the event of a serious crisis, the application of export refunds should be activated on a temporary basis. these proposals highlight the fundamental shortcomings of the union's crisis management and affect the functioning of the market for all product lines.

in writing. there are doubts about the transparency of the eu's workings, which have been raised in the eu institutions in recent months in the context of ttip. but the story started on a positive note: last year, the commission launched a public debate on the dispute settlement mechanism of the free trade agreement, where more than 150 000 people participated, 97% of whom said no to isds, supporting the eu not to give foreign investors preferences over national governments or authorities. in a few months, the european civil initiative 'stop ttip' has gathered over two million signatures in 14 member states, obliging the commission to give a formal response to a proposal to suspend ttip negotiations and abandon the isds, which must be heard by the european parliament. but it seems that too many big business interests are at stake for the opinion of eu citizens to be decisive. the two largest groups in the ep, the epp and the s&d, adopted a report with the parliament which, by rewriting the original proposal, did not explicitly reject isds, and indeed, with a repackaging trick set up as a compromise, the socialists are actually going to support the commission's pro-isds position. in view of the above, it is right for supporters of european democracy to ask: where is the point in the ttip negotiations where the opinion of citizens becomes unavoidable against business interests, and who are those who are preparing to adopt rules that are contrary to the position of european citizens?
in writing. the us free trade agreement, which has clear benefits for europe and hungary, has been hampered for months by political sentiment and hysteria surrounding the investor state dispute settlement mechanism. calm down, my fellow mps. the dispute mechanism is not going to destroy our planet, it's not going to tear apart the european legal order, and it's not going to force us to eat genetically modified hamburgers from now on. this is clear from the commission's public negotiating mandate. the commission has also provided the commission with a report on the implementation of the new rules on the protection of personal data. the dispute settlement mechanism shall not compel any member state to legislate contrary to the interests of its citizens. investors cannot force us to grow genetically modified food, to weaken environmental protection, to weaken workers' or consumers' rights. on the other hand, deliberate misinterpretation causes serious damage to the people of europe and hungary. without a us free trade agreement, european and hungarian families could lose $160,000 a year in savings. without a deal, europe will lose two million jobs, hungary 30,000, and the eastern european periphery will remain totally dependent on russian energy. without an agreement, without a north atlantic economic alliance of 850 million, europe's place in the world economy will be further weakened. if there is no agreement, we could one day find ourselves with the global economic rules dictated by asia and latin america. those who are stirring up political hysteria should do so with a careful balance of the above.
in writing. ttip can be an important tool in regulating globalisation and improving the eu's international competitiveness, but this requires a number of legal, political and economic framework conditions. the european parliament should therefore exercise active political control and direction throughout the negotiations leading to ttip, and its activities should not be limited to the forthcoming final vote. this can be a guarantee that the agreement will ultimately generate real jobs and growth in europe, without prejudice to eu labour, social, environmental and consumer protection standards. in implementing the negotiating directives drawn up with the member states and the ep, the commission representatives must also bear in mind and enforce this complex set of conditions, as it is the agreement's meaning in terms of european interests. i believe that the existing isds mechanism and the solution to ensure that the opaque and abusive practices surrounding it are eliminated - essentially the creation of a new public system under transparent and democratic control - also deserve support, because this will provide the commission with a clear negotiating framework for the next round of negotiations, which will serve the european interest.

in writing. ‒ in line with the guidelines of the european people's party, i voted in favour of the report on fishing rights for venezuelan fishing vessels. this report also makes it clear that the european union is obliged to limit its sea fishing to the extent necessary to maintain marine fish stocks. 30% of the world's oceans are overfished, and marine fish stocks are in danger. the reasoned measures taken to maintain them have led to a continuous and significant decline in the amount of marine fish caught. the cfp should therefore pay much more attention to sustainable fisheries, i.e. aquaculture, and in particular freshwater fisheries. a significant part of the hungarian wetlands is located in natura 2000 areas. these fish farms do not represent any threat to the natural values of these areas. in fact, in many cases it is our closed systems of wetlands that have created and preserved unique associations of aquatic habitats. consequently, freshwater aquaculture should be freed from unnecessarily stringent and unnecessary sustainability standards that are justified only for marine fisheries. efforts should be made to define and regulate freshwater aquaculture clearly now.
in writing. ‒ for decades, venezuelan fishing vessels have been fishing under licence in eu waters off the coast of french guiana, in return for landing part of their catch in local ports. the landing and processing of fishery products is a source of income and a significant source of employment in french guiana. however, in the absence of an international fisheries agreement between the eu and venezuela, this situation is contrary to the requirements of the community legal order. the proposal aims to bring about a legal solution to this situation.

in writing. ‒ the commission proposes, on the basis of point 11 of the interinstitutional agreement of 2 december 2013, to mobilise the european union solidarity fund (eusf) in connection with the floods in romania (spring and summer 2014), bulgaria (summer 2014) and italy (autumn 2013). the commission carried out a thorough examination of all four applications. in all four cases, the commission proposes to take account of 2,5% of the total direct damage, as no region has reached the threshold for a 'significant disaster'. this is in line with the previous practice for regional disasters and disasters supported under the neighbourhood provision. the total proposed mobilisation is eur 66 505 850. on the basis of the above, as a member of the hungarian people's party delegation, i supported the adoption of the proposal in agreement with the european people's party.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report as it makes important findings and suggestions concerning the fruit and vegetable sector in hungary and the eu. as is well known, the 2007 reform aimed to strengthen producer organisations in the sector, on the one hand by providing a wider range of tools to prevent and manage market risks, and on the other by improving and concentrating supply, increasing quality and competitiveness, adapting supply to the market and providing technical support for environmentally friendly production. i agree that the european commission's report gives a balanced picture of the development of the sector since the 2007 reform, and a realistic picture of the problems that remain. the report rightly calls on the commission to step up its efforts to tackle unfair trading practices in the food supply chain and to take further steps to protect producers. i agree that it is necessary to continue to support producer organisations, to maintain european quality standards and to promote european quality and standardisation elements in negotiations with third countries. the report is therefore an important step towards harmonising and helping the eu fruit and vegetable sector, but i believe that the system will only be fully harmonised and solidarity based when member states cannot tax our food too much.
on behalf of the ppe group.– mr president, we often say here in the house that europe is in a difficult phase, a difficult situation in its history. this week i think we can rightly say this, but that underlines the fact that we have to work on the effectiveness of how our union works. the exercise of discussing the commission’s work programme is something like that. let us go back a little bit. i am glad that the vice-president started with a little stocktaking because, here in the middle of the year, we can already see what has been happening. on behalf of the epp i can confirm that the commission has made a quick start and a good start. the investment package and many other initiatives have been strong, and on behalf of parliament we would like to help this process of going forward in these areas. this energetic start should go on. i also would like to comment on the point that many have misinterpreted parliament’s decision in january about the lack of support or a resolution on the commission’s work programme. normally in election years this is not required, because planning is much longer and much more preparation is needed, so it is not a failure to meet our obligations. but this year is a full year, which means that we can already have full preparation, which we are doing. obviously, i am not saying that the preparation process is perfect. for example, in the negotiations which we are now having here in parliament, we have had to discuss all the things which had been done in this last half year – all the compromises which we are going to foresee in the next year and the second part of this year – which are a little bit too dense, which means that we cannot make the same kind of compromises. however, in exercise of parliament’s very important power, which is the right of initiative, we have this instrument which we have to use in order to get some kind of ideas on the commission table, and we expect the commission to follow those. the first thing is the method. i am glad that the vice-president has mentioned that we want effective legislation, fighting red tape (including a significant reduction of the cost of the bureaucratic burden), and the transposition, implementation and enforcement of eu legislation. very often we do not need new legislation; we just need to implement that which already exists in the right way. it obviously should not be a question of vanity whether someone has a report or a piece of legislation. we have to look more thoroughly in this parliament at whether we can do more with a view to implementation. the commission has to do the same. so this is why we are fully supporting the better law-making exercise and law-making programme. another very important matter is the alignment of the legislation to the delegated and implementing act provisions of the lisbon treaty. this is a big delay; the lisbon treaty has been in force for quite a long time. we have seen resistance on the part of the council. the commission should also help parliament to have full rights in this, otherwise we are falling into a constant inter-institutional fight in this area. we should solve this problem; it is already impossible that we have not gone further ahead on this. unfortunately, the commission has withdrawn this piece of legislation. we hope that in the framework of the better law-making package we can do more. in our view, jobs remain the top priority; mobility and flexibility of the labour market have to be improved, as well as youth employment. the digital agenda has to play a crucial role in our society, especially in creating and re-shoring jobs, improving skills of eu citizens and work and school for the younger generation, giving better access to digital services. the next development of the emu should be based, in our view, on the existing two-pack and six-pack legislation. we are against any revision of these two main instruments for the moment; we want them to be fully implemented and applied. on taxation policy, which is an integral part of the structural reform of the member states, we would like to see a development, a shift of the tax burden from labour to other forms of taxation. concerning the eu budget, the fight against tax fraud and evasion, supporting the better performance of the eu budget, is something very important. so just to sum up, we would now like parliament to say that we want to have a say in this exercise, and this is what our resolution, hopefully, will be there to do. i hope that many colleagues in this house can support the joint resolutions which we have prepared.
the european commission's new programme clearly states that it supports legal forms of migration and that it will take strong action against illegal migration. i ask you to make a clear distinction between the two here in public. explain to european citizens what legal and illegal migration is. what we do know is that legal migration is obviously when someone is fleeing war, seeking asylum. i ask why such a person would destroy and throw away his passport, his identity documents, on the serbian side of the schengen hungarian-serbian border, why he would not present his passport and say, "please, i come from syria, from a war zone, i am in danger of my life, please declare me a refugee". my second question is: how can people who come from muslim countries leave behind their female family members, their wives, their children, their mothers in a life-threatening war situation? i'd like an explanation for that, which you obviously have official knowledge of.
the eu emissions trading scheme was introduced to ensure the eu's commitment to reduce emissions in a cost-effective way. the 2020 target is automatically guaranteed by the total quota. all interventions in the functioning of the market, including the stabilisation reserve, are necessary because of over-fulfillment. because of ambition, while the eu is responsible for only 9% of global emissions. after 2020, the free quota would be reserved for the most efficient installations. that is, a power plant or steel plant that has made all the possible improvements with the technology in question, but not the most advanced one available, becomes uncompetitive and may close down by paying the expensive quota. tens of thousands of jobs will be lost, the flow of imports will come from ukraine, steel from india, where they don't care about carbon emissions. is that what we want?

in writing. i was pleased to read in the luxembourg presidency's programme that energy issues were to be addressed in the next six months. among the different dimensions of the energy union, the presidency highlighted the area of research, development and innovation. these are really important questions that we need to address. we probably haven't talked about them much. at the same time, i hope that other important areas of energy policy, such as infrastructure development, the bi-directionalisation of pipelines or diversification, will not be overlooked. we've just made it through a winter without a gas crisis, but surely none of us want to have to worry about the next plot. ensuring the security of energy supply is still the number one energy policy mandate for all responsible european leaders today. tomorrow we will not live in a world of smart metering and decentralized energy production. we must do everything we can to spread these technologies, but in the meantime we must ensure a continuous supply of energy. i therefore ask the luxembourg presidency to focus on the pressing problems of the present, alongside the challenges of the future, in the field of energy policy. in this work, you can count on the european parliament, which has just begun to discuss the commission's proposal for an energy union.
in writing. i think it is important that the eu leaders have recognised that not only the problems of accommodating people rescued at sea need to be tackled jointly, but that the problem of those arriving on land also needs to be addressed quickly. hungary has been hit by a wave of immigration that is the highest in europe in terms of population. just last weekend, over 2,000 asylum seekers were registered, bringing the total to 70,000 this year. this year's wave of immigration is not a special event of war, the result of persecution, which is limited in time, space, number, finite. europe has faced these problems before, but it has managed them well. the current wave of migration, due to its scale and scope, is about to create an unmanageable situation. the unresolved issues of immigration that we have to face are the biggest challenges for our children and even our grandchildren. so we need less generous flattery today and more responsible, forward-looking action. statistics show that many more are arriving who, in the hope of better living, are giving up everything to enter the promised europe. the actual number of refugees is much lower. we need to find a solution with the appropriate sensitivity and empathy, so that those who are really in need receive the right help, but not as an invitation to tens of thousands more. only in this way can the member states protect their borders, ensure the normal course of life and preserve this europe in the long term.
it is the responsibility and duty of all of us to protect the lives, dignity and fundamental rights of people everywhere in the world. the attacks that have occurred in recent times are terrifying in their reality and in their symbolism, for they send the message that any of us, anywhere in the world, can be a victim. there is no acceptable explanation for such actions, so we must use all means to prevent them. one of the tasks we have to do is to work together, to look for partners in the world, as the commissioner has said. we need to harness the resources available, trained, effective law enforcement to protect our safety and our values. we need to prevent the radicalization of young adults in our normal societies. at the same time, let me also speak about the innocent victims who are persecuted for their faith, and i am thinking here of the christians, many of them women and children, who are today victims of the atrocities of isis. they are the martyrs of our century. in addition to the human losses, we must also speak out against the destruction of priceless monuments dating back thousands of years in regions known as the cradle of our civilization. we'll have less of a humanity.

in writing. we must continue to stand united against the increasing violence and killings in the middle east by daesh against religious minorities, including christians. the european union is a leader in helping refugees. it is also our moral duty in europe to further increase our efforts to protect the persecuted. the effectiveness of the aid is greatly enhanced by the critical efforts of local churches in support of christian and other indigenous minorities persecuted by the dáis. without them, the rise of radical islam in the middle east would have been a catastrophe long ago. i'll give you concrete examples: the chaldean catholic church in northern iraq is now responsible for the daily care of hundreds of thousands of refugees, or the jesuit refugee service in syria. most of this is financed by their own funds and by international church donations. churches run successful projects and reach out directly to those who need it most. however, the current eu aid procedure does not consider local churches as partners and prevents their direct participation in european aid projects. it is essential that the institutions of the union responsible for aid and development see the professional church aid organisations as partners in humanitarian action. we can't afford to leave the people who are most affected by this situation out of the loop. the eu's decision-makers urgently need to think together to overcome the humanitarian crisis together with local partners.
on behalf of the verts/ale group.– mr president, first of all i would like to thank mr kukan for the exemplary collegial and cooperative attitude with which he steered through a difficult and wide-ranging report. i personally enjoyed our work immensely and i thank you for that, mr kukan, together with the shadow rapporteurs. i rarely enjoy the luxury of two-and-a-half minutes’ leisurely time, but nevertheless i want to concentrate on one aspect which unfortunately was left out of the report. i would like to try to convince those who are still with me on the merits of it. we are all supportive of differentiation, flexibility, efficacy and coherence in our policies towards our neighbours. this is natural for us as well. we offer our full support for all measures that could strengthen our common policies. however, the valued principle of ‘more for more’ squares badly with conditionality and coherence once we observe that some of our neighbours happen to backtrack on development towards democracy. what are the options that we are left with if one of the neighbouring countries happens to imprison some political opponents or threaten them with the death penalty? as much as we like soft power – and its best expression is ‘more for more’, and we agree on that – unless we are able to say that we are going to offer less for less if backtracking takes place, then our policies are not going to be highly coherent. this is very important because our neighbourhood policies, as the report itself shows, have produced mixed results at best in the last couple of years. the failed state of libya and the less-than-half success of the eastern partnership show that the new challenges in our immediate environment need new responses. these new responses are enumerated in the report and we offer support for all those measures. i would like to end by asking colleagues to support this report with their votes.
mr president, one of my young political memories is of the helsinki conference in 1975, which launched the process of european de-escalation and triggered what can be described as almost revolutionary changes in the field of human and minority rights. the helsinki process, which began 40 years ago, led directly to the collapse of soviet communism and, as a result, to the dismantling of the iron curtain and the emergence of the democratic europe of today. it is a curious twist of fate that russia, one of the founding members of the osce, cannot celebrate the anniversary of the historic helsinki final act with the other founding members. we are witnessing a serious decline in peace, security, dialogue and cooperation, as the initial encouraging results of the european neighbourhood policy have meanwhile backfired. the eu's eastern partnership policy has been in a permanent crisis, in particular as a result of the retreating soviet imperial legacy. the situation now in place fully justifies the strategic need to review our european neighbourhood policy. the interests of both the european union and the european partnership countries require a renewal of our neighbourhood policy based on the european values of fundamental human rights, the rule of law, democracy, freedom and human dignity. finally, may i congratulate mr. kukan on his excellent work.
mr president, looking back at the past, i am reminded of the year 2012, when the european union won the nobel peace prize. and then three years passed, and in the neighborhood of a peaceful europe, a nobel peace prize winning europe, we saw flames. of these, perhaps the most mentioned today is the ukrainian crisis, although it should be added that these crises in any part of our neighbourhood are not just in themselves, they are not because something has gone wrong in one country or another, but, i think, they have broader contexts, so it is high time that we undertook a comprehensive and conceptual review of our neighbourhood policy. i believe, mr president, that this neighbourhood policy cannot succeed if europe is not united. i am a little bit disappointed that we have two very, very well-trained commissioners, mr hahn and mrs mogherini, who are dealing with these issues and are being replaced by other european leaders in most cases, although it is obvious that what they are doing is not useless either. but we need unity, and that includes not making friends with our opponents in certain eu member states - i can even think of the friendship between orbán and putin. so i think the real stake of the neighbourhood policy is how europe can deal with it, and i'm afraid we're going to have to work on that nobel peace prize a second time, this time in the neighbourhood.
in writing.– recent events call for immediate solutions, and intensive communications are needed between eu and neighbourhood countries. the eu has to implement appropriate treatment of the neighbourhood countries’ claims, take common responsibility, inspire the judicial, economic, social reforms, the fight against corruption, and pay attention to the rights of the national minorities in the partner countries. for example, as a first step of the administration reform in ukraine, the law ‘on voluntary association of local authorities/communities’ was adopted in which point 4, article 4 states that during the administrative reforms the historical, linguistic and ethnic characteristics have to be taken into account. the related article of the regulation provides an opportunity for the national minorities to organise at the municipal level. however the 11th article of the government’s resolution containing the implementation of the law does not include directives considering the ethnic aspects as it is in the law, which can affect detrimentally the national minorities. it is very important to modify the government’s resolution as soon as possible according to the law and considering the rights of the national minorities living in ukraine. i therefore call on the eu to pay necessary attention to the necessary reforms in ukraine and other neighbourhood countries.

mr president, i voted against the document which would allow for a free trade agreement between the eu and the usa. because, of course, if someone takes seriously the fact that we, the directly elected representatives, represent the interests of the population, then they could only vote no, because those who voted yes represent the interests of the multinational companies. the two economies are not in the same weight class, europe can only lose. it is a big delusion that small and medium-sized european enterprises are the focus, 87% of them produce for the domestic market, the internal market. do they get to america? no, i'm not going. the american companies with the capital, the aggressive marketing, they're taking away the opportunity. and by the way, it's misleading that the dispute resolution mechanism is now solved. not a private court, but a court created by a vague proposal, we don't know what kind of court allows these companies to sue sovereign states for their lost profits.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the motion for a resolution because i believe that the european parliament should exercise active political control and direction throughout the negotiations for ttip, and our decision today is an important element of this. the ttip can be an important tool in regulating globalisation processes and improving the eu's international competitiveness, but this requires a number of legal, political and economic framework conditions, which are duly laid down in this resolution and thus set the tone for the commission's negotiations with the us side. i believe that as the negotiations progress, the ep should have more discussions and resolutions of this kind, in particular with a view to ensuring that the agreement will lead to a better global competitive position for the eu and, ultimately, to real jobs and growth in europe, without prejudice to eu labour, social, environmental and consumer protection standards. the resolution also has the important merit of providing a compromise solution to the existing isds mechanism and its inherent opaque practices that disadvantage individual investors or governments, by creating a new, transparent and democratically controlled public system. the ep has thus contributed to the commission's ability to have a clear negotiating framework for the next round of negotiations on this highly controversial issue, which serves european interests.

in writing. ‒ the fidesz delegation of the epp, in agreement with the epp, is committed to improving the economic environment in the european union. the objective is to achieve cost-efficiency, reduce the administrative burden on operators in order to increase competitiveness. job creation is primarily the responsibility of companies and not governments, and this requires clear rules, but achieving transparency cannot mean increasing the operating costs of european economic organisations. it is essential to establish the framework conditions, both economic and legal, which enable and facilitate the stimulation of the economy and the creation of new jobs. this was the aim of the report adopted today, especially when the remuneration policy and the long-term commitment of shareholders are at stake. however, i did not support the so-called country-by-country reporting in the report, as i do not believe that a reporting obligation similar to the oecd's rules on the large enterprise tax avoidance exemption (beps) has a place in sectoral legislation similar to this directive.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report on the amendment of directive 2007/36/ec to encourage long-term shareholder engagement and directive 2013/34/eu as regards certain elements of the corporate governance statement. these are fundamental principles that encourage shareholders to be more involved and interested in long-term planning rather than short-term planning, which often leads to serious damage and underfunding. it is appropriate that, in order to facilitate this, the directive requires greater transparency as regards the identity of shareholders, since direct contact and closer cooperation can only be achieved by identifying shareholders. i welcome the addition of an additional disclosure requirement that large companies should disclose in the notes to the financial statements the relevant information on the tax assessment, broken down by member state and third country where these large companies have a subsidiary. the amendment also contributes to sustainability by requiring issuers to publish additional data pertaining to the financial year (such as turnover, profit before tax, tax on profit or public subsidies received) on an annual basis, on a country-by-country basis, on an aggregated basis. the inclusion of this in the report is one of the most important achievements of the socialists. the amendments to strengthen the exercise of rights attaching to shares will certainly have a positive impact on the capital investment regime within the union.
in writing. ‒ it is important that the eu ets promotes low-carbon growth and protects the competitiveness of eu sectors that are at significant risk of carbon leakage. the european council conclusions on the 2030 climate and energy framework provided clear guidance that the free allocation and cap-and-trade provisions should be maintained beyond 2020. on the basis of those strategic guidelines, the commission should review directive 2003/87/ec, and in particular article 10a thereof, and propose a revision of that directive within six months of the adoption of this decision. in order to ensure a level playing field, the review will also examine the harmonised rules for compensating indirect costs at union level. the review should also consider the appropriateness of using up to 50 million unallocated allowances before 2021 to complement existing resources to promote projects referred to in article 10a (8) of that directive and low-carbon industrial innovation projects, including smaller scale projects, across all member states. in view of the above, i voted in favour of the adoption of the report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report, as i consider the importance of a well-functioning and stable eu ets to be key. i welcome the effort to achieve the objective of the scheme, which is to encourage cost-effective and economically viable reductions in greenhouse gas emissions. the report adopted today also aims at achieving stability and sustainable emissions trading. i consider it of paramount importance to address the excess emissions and to address the deficiencies in the system in order to achieve the target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 2020 and to achieve long-term cost-effectiveness. furthermore, i agree with the rapporteur that there is an urgent need for further discussion on improving the allocation of free allowances so that the most efficient installations do not have to bear unjustified carbon costs, as this would lead to emissions trading.
in writing. ‒ the ets has generated an estimated surplus of more than 2 billion emission allowances since 2009. this surplus is reflected in the supply of emission allowances, thereby reducing the price of carbon emissions, which in turn constrains investment in low-carbon technologies. the european parliament called on the commission back in 2012 to adopt measures to correct the shortcomings of the ets. the commission's 2014 proposal to create a market stabilisation reserve is a structural reform that complements the emissions trading system directive with new rules to control market fluctuations and in particular the supply of allowances. i support this reform.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report because i think that the creation of a reserve is a good solution. as we know, the purpose of emissions trading is to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. however, the supply-demand balance of emission allowances has been upset, and this is now hampering green investment. power plants, airlines, companies are free to trade in emission quotas, which determine how much pollutants can be released into the air. quotas are currently very cheap as demand has decreased, partly due to the economic crisis. however, there was no movement on the supply side. in 2013, there was a surplus of more than 2 billion on the quota market compared to current emissions, which could exceed 2.6 billion by 2020. a quota is one ton of carbon dioxide. the surplus reduces the willingness to invest green and may thus also jeopardise the effectiveness of the ets. in my view, this move sends a strong message to the eu's climate policy, which is also of great importance in view of the upcoming paris climate summit. i believe that a stable and flexible system is needed to create a more predictable situation for the member states and the market. i would point out that in developing the stability reserve, it is important to encourage further investment and to ensure consistency with other climate and energy policies.
in writing. ‒ the european commission's proposal aims to improve working conditions for seafarers on board ships flying the flag of one of the 28 member states of the european union, including taking account of the specificities of the sector. the proposal was designed to harmonise the six directives on employment and social dialogue which had not previously covered seafarers. the directives on the insolvency of employers, the european works council, the reduction of the number of employees in a group and the protection of workers' rights in the event of the transfer of undertakings have thus been revised. the ep amendments concern mainly the area of social dialogue and cooperation. the amendments adopted may be important for me and for hungarian citizens working abroad, on the high seas, despite the fact that the regulations have no significant direct, territorial impact on hungary. the people's party approach was particularly important for us in the following areas and policy areas: disproportionate costs, administrative or legal restrictions that would impede the creation and development of small and medium-sized enterprises and family businesses should not be supported; seafarers should not be discriminated against on the basis of their eu citizenship; and the security of on-board communication devices should be increased.
in writing. the european commission's proposal aims to improve working conditions for seafarers on board ships flying the flag of one of the 28 member states of the european union, including taking account of the specificities of the sector. the proposal was designed to harmonise the six directives on employment and social dialogue which had not previously covered seafarers. the directives on insolvency of employers, on the european works council, on group redundancies and on the protection of workers' rights in the event of transfers of undertakings have thus been revised. the ep amendments concern mainly the area of social dialogue and cooperation with regard to the working conditions and safety of seafarers. i followed the people's party's position because the report managed to incorporate amendments that may be important for me and for hungarian citizens working abroad, even though the regulations have no significant direct, territorial impact on hungary. the people's party approach was particularly important for us in the following areas and policy areas: disproportionate costs, administrative or legal restrictions that would impede the creation and development of small and medium-sized enterprises and family businesses should not be supported; seafarers should not be discriminated against on the basis of their eu nationality; and the security of on-board communication devices should be increased.

mr president, with the successful delegation of our colleague, mr deva, who is also present in this room, we went to south korea a few weeks ago, where i was able to see for myself what the secret is of how a very poor, miserable country became one of the most successful nations and states in the world. they were following the same path that my country, hungary, should have followed after the so-called regime change instead of being made into a big assembly plant. in south korea, they focused on training, innovation, technology development, and manufacturing their own products that they could produce. i would call this a genuine employment policy, and to have an economy that is commensurate with the capabilities of each member state and creates jobs that correspond to those capabilities, for example in hungary.
in writing. ‒ each year, the european commission prepares and the european council (in the framework of epsco) discusses the so-called employment policy directives for the member states. since the public employment system was introduced in hungary, it has been continuously criticized by the european commission, although the legacy in this area is particularly serious. the latest analysis of the hungarian central statistical office (ksh), which operates according to european standards, in april 2015 found that the number of unemployed people increased by 150,000 between 2001 and 2011. at the same time, the most developed eu countries (e.g. denmark, luxembourg) have also experienced a dramatic increase in the number of low-skilled unemployed, which needs to be addressed in the short term. this was also recognised by the european parliament in its report. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work. hungary is now at the forefront of europe in reducing unemployment, a fact that is increasingly recognised.
in writing. the latest analysis of the hungarian central statistical office (ksh) based on european standards, in april 2015, found that the number of unemployed people increased by 150,000 between 2001 and 2011. at the time of the 2010 change of government, hungary had the highest level of education, with almost 30% of the unemployed having completed primary school or less, which was about 170,000 people. around the time of accession to the eu, the situation of unskilled people worsened by almost 100 000 in 2001-2004, and then further from 2008-2009, with 98 000 unemployed in one year. a year later, between 2009 and 2010, another 93,000 people lost their jobs among people with low education. at the same time, the most developed eu countries (e.g. denmark, luxembourg) have also experienced a dramatic increase in the number of low-skilled unemployed people, which needs to be addressed in the short term, as recognised by the european parliament in this report. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work. hungary is now at the forefront of europe in reducing unemployment, a fact that is increasingly recognised. the amendment tabled by mr adam kos also drew attention to this, and the committee on employment and social affairs supported it, so i voted in favour of the final version of the report.

in writing. ‒ each year, the european commission prepares and the european council (in the framework of epsco) discusses the so-called employment policy directives for the member states. since the public employment system was introduced in hungary, it has been continuously criticized by the european commission, although the legacy in this area is particularly serious. the latest analysis of the hungarian central statistical office (ksh), which operates according to european standards, in april 2015 found that the number of unemployed people increased by 150,000 between 2001 and 2011. at the time of the 2010 change of government, hungary had the highest level of education, with almost 30% of the unemployed having completed primary school or less, which was about 170,000 people. around the time of accession to the eu, the situation of unskilled people worsened by almost 100 000 in 2001-2004, and then again from 2008-2009 when 98 000 people lost their jobs in one year. a year later, in 2009-2010, another 93,000 people lost their jobs among people with low education. at the same time, the most developed eu countries (e.g. denmark, luxembourg) have also experienced a dramatic increase in the number of low-skilled unemployed people, which needs to be addressed in the short term, as recognised by the european parliament in this report.

in writing. ‒ each year, the european commission prepares and the european council (in the framework of epsco) discusses the so-called employment policy directives for the member states. since the public employment system was introduced in hungary, it has been criticised by the european commission, although the legacy is particularly severe, and at the same time the number of low-skilled unemployed has increased dramatically in the most developed eu countries (e.g. denmark, luxembourg), which needs to be addressed in the short term, as the european parliament has acknowledged in this report. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work. hungary is now at the forefront of europe in reducing unemployment, a fact that is increasingly recognised. the amendment tabled by mr adam kos also drew attention to this, and the committee on employment and social affairs supported it, so i voted in favour of the final version of the report.
in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the report because it makes useful employment policy proposals to the european commission and the european council. the report stresses the need to coordinate training across sectors at eu level and to develop a common strategy. i agree that the union should accompany these efforts with policy proposals to achieve the objectives of the treaty and to ensure inclusive, integrated labour markets and fair working conditions including adequate remuneration through collective bargaining throughout the union. the report states that at least 20 million people need to be lifted out of poverty and exclusion. therefore, it seems necessary to establish reliable indicators of the conditions of extreme poverty experienced by many eu citizens even today. i think it's important to have these indicators, and i regret to say that the hungarian government, in the opposite direction, refuses to measure the indicators that reflect the situation of those living in poverty. i share the view that one of the eu's most important tasks is to create a fairer, more inclusive, rights-based labour market based on social protection. i also consider it important to note that, in order to combat extreme poverty and social exclusion, these actions should include social protection measures such as the guaranteed minimum income, to be introduced in accordance with national practices.
in writing. ‒ on 2 june 2015, the commission adopted a proposal for a decision to mobilise the european globalisation adjustment fund for finland to support the reintegration into the labour market of workers made redundant by broadcom and two suppliers or downstream companies. according to the finnish authorities, the reason for the redundancies at broadcom was that it was closing all its activities in finland. this closure is linked to the significant structural changes in the structure of world trade due to globalisation, recalling that in 2004 asia became the largest employer in the electronics and electricity sectors. this has led to a decrease in the number of european workers. as regards the domestic situation, the finnish authorities point to a trend in the finnish electronics sector as a whole, culminating in the mass redundancies announced by nokia in 2011. the commission considers that the measures described above constitute active labour market measures falling within the scope of the eligible activities. on the basis of the above, and in view of the interinstitutional agreement of 2 december 2015, i, as a member of the hungarian people's party delegation, supported the adoption of the proposal in agreement with the european people's party.
in writing. on 2 june 2015, the commission adopted a proposal for a decision to mobilise the european globalisation adjustment fund for finland to support the reintegration into the labour market of workers made redundant by broadcom and two suppliers or downstream companies. according to the finnish authorities, the reason for the redundancies at broadcom was that it was closing all its activities in finland. this closure is linked to the significant structural changes in the structure of world trade due to globalisation, recalling that in 2004 asia became the largest employer in the electronics and electricity sectors. this has led to a decrease in the number of european workers. as regards the domestic situation, the finnish authorities point to a trend in the finnish electronics sector as a whole, culminating in the mass redundancies announced by nokia in 2011. the personalised services to be provided to redundant workers consist of three types of measures: (i) helping them to find new jobs; (ii) helping them to start their own business and (iii) providing them with training or education. the commission considers that the measures described above constitute active labour market measures falling within the scope of the eligible activities. on the basis of the above, in view of the interinstitutional agreement of 2 december 2015, the hungarian people's party delegation supported the adoption of the proposal in agreement with the european people's party.

in writing. ‒ i voted in favour of the commission's proposal for a decision to mobilise the european globalisation adjustment fund for the benefit of finland. it is crucial that this is the twelfth application to be examined under the 2015 budget and that it is directed to the mobilisation of a total of eur 1 365 000 from the egf for the benefit of finland. it affects 500 of the 568 workers made redundant by broadcom and two of its suppliers. it should be noted that according to the finnish authorities, the reason for the redundancies at broadcom was that it was closing all its activities in finland. this closure is linked to the significant structural changes in the structure of world trade due to globalisation, recalling that in the 2000s the finnish subsidiaries increased their staffing levels on all continents, while in 2004 asia became the largest employer in the electronics and electricity sectors. this has led to a decrease in the number of european workers. as regards the domestic situation, the finnish authorities point to a trend in the finnish electronics sector as a whole, culminating in the mass redundancies announced by nokia in 2011. the report adopted today was also intended to remedy this situation and to ensure sustainable operation.
in writing. ‒ the european globalisation adjustment fund aims to provide support for workers affected by the consequences of major structural changes in world trade or made redundant as a result of the global financial and economic crisis, and to support their reintegration into the labour market. finland submitted its application for a financial contribution from the egf following 568 redundancies at broadcom communications finland and two suppliers or downstream companies. as the application meets the eligibility criteria set out in the egf regulation, i supported the submission.
in writing. ‒ the european parliament today adopted by a large majority its mandate for the negotiations on the eu budget for 2016. in preparation for the negotiations with the council, meps confirmed that cohesion policy remains a priority for the european parliament. as a member of the hungarian people's party, i believe that the eu needs to quickly clear its multi-billion euro deficit on development projects, and the 2016 eu budget can be an important tool for this. as in previous years, the mandate for negotiations with the council focuses on cohesion policy and the preservation of the resources of the common agricultural policy. if the council decides to reduce these during the budgetary procedure, we are prepared to defend budget lines which are important for hungarian interests by submitting amendment proposals. on the basis of the above, and in view of the interinstitutional agreement of 2 december 2015, i, as a member of the hungarian people's party delegation, supported the adoption of the proposal in agreement with the european people's party.

mr president, i am of course in favour of so-called green employment, the creation of green jobs, but i find it particularly cynical that the european union should initiate and enforce this, which has ruined agriculture in so many countries, including my own, hungary. recently, as i mentioned, i was at hortobagy, where i was able to see firsthand how direct subsidies, that is, land-based subsidies, how the manipulation of these subsidies destroys the ecological balance, how they destroy livestock, and how they further destroy agriculture, in addition to the destruction that the eu has already done by opening up our markets and sending food from the other side of the world to hungary and other european countries. under these circumstances, it may be considered cynical to talk about green employment.
in writing. ‒ the commission's green jobs initiative, which builds on the concept of the circular economy presented in the green action plan for smes (also included in this report) published last year, aims to create up to 20 million jobs in the green economy by 2020, including in health and so-called green jobs. one of the biggest challenges is that it is estimated that 95% of fresh produce in certain food chains will be threatened by climate change, and a third will be at serious risk. significant progress is also needed in the area of energy efficiency, as efforts are being made in the country to increase the energy efficiency of residential buildings, and further efforts are needed in the area of awareness raising, such as environmental education and training. this should include strengthening education in general, in particular to develop skills in science, technology and mathematics. i also support the approach of involving disadvantaged workers in the creation of such jobs. i supported the people's party's position on critical issues, in particular to reduce the burden on smes and thus on family businesses, and to ensure adequate and fair preparation time for the transition to a green economy.
